title: Chapter II
focus: the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party

teacherSummary.text: Between West Egg and New York lies a valley of ashes, overseen by the faded billboard eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. Tom takes Nick to George Wilson's garage there and brings Wilson's wife, Myrtle, into the city to the apartment he keeps for her. At a drunken party with Myrtle's sister Catherine and the McKees, Myrtle buys a dog and puts on airs. When she shouts Daisy's name, Tom breaks her nose with his open hand.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party. writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter II suggests about the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's setting and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald uses setting in Chapter II to complicate the reader's understanding of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter II within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter II and its treatment of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's setting and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter II as evidence for a larger claim about the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party in The Great Gatsby. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter II as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the valley of ashes and Myrtle's party. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Great Gatsby.

Tom takes Nick to George Wilson's garage there and brings Wilson's wife, Myrtle, into the city to the apartment he keeps for her. At a drunken party with Myrtle's sister Catherine…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

items.text: How does “Chapter II” build on “Chapter I”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The valley of ashes shows the human cost hidden beneath the glamour of the Eggs. Useful evidence: “The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are blue and gigantic” (Chapter II, paragraph 2): The billboard eyes. Theme link: Myrtle tries to buy her way into Tom's world (a dog, a flat, a new dress); Wilson is drained of life. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The valley of ashes shows the human cost hidden beneath the glamour of the Eggs. Useful evidence: “Making a short deft movement, Tom Buchanan broke her nose with his open hand” (Chapter II, paragraph 127): Tom's casual violence. On characterization: Tom's violence: he breaks Myrtle's nose with his open hand. middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Tom breaks Myrtle's nose. Some students may have experienced violence at home; keep focus on what the act reveals about power and class.
